newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germans optimistic despite weaker Ifo survey.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germans optimistic despite weaker Ifo survey.

text.p: German business sentiment worsened in March according to a survey by the Ifo research institute but analysts said the recovery remained on track and predicted the mood would brighten in coming months.

The closely watched Ifo business climate index for west Germany fell to 92.4 in March from 93.6 in February, confounding market expectations of a slight rise to 94.0. The east German index was unchanged at 104.1.
The news had surprisingly little impact on German Bunds, which rose only briefly and quickly pared their gains, but it helped lift the dollar against the mark.
Separately, the Federal Statistics Office said German retail sales fell 6.0 percent in February in price-adjusted terms compared with the year-earlier month.

But economists paid closer attention to the month-on-month comparison which showed a rise of 0.2 percent in seasonally-adjusted and price-adjusted terms. That gain was regarded as encouraging as it came on top of a steep 2.7 percent rise in January.
The pace of Germany's recovery this year is crucial to its chances of qualifying for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), scheduled to go ahead in 1999.

The government's forecast of a 1997 budget deficit just below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- the ceiling for candidates wishing to adopt the single currency -- is based on the assumption that the economy will grow by 2.5 percent this year.
Despite Thursday's data, economists said that growth forecast still seems realistic provided that the mark does not appreciate sharply in the course of the year.
"The Ifo index fall is just a temporary phenomenon, nothing that indicates a new trend," said Hans-Juergen Meltzer, an economist at Deutsche Bank Research. "I think it will be reversed in April."
Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at Trinkaus & Burkhardt, said the fall was not particularly surprising because the dollar weakened slightly in March.
Sentiment was also likely to have been hit by persistent uncertainty about the outcome of political wrangling about planned corporate tax reforms, Kricks-Brunnlieb said.
Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley said the drop was explained by the unusually low number of working days in March, which this year contained part of the Easter holiday.
With just 19 days worked compared with the normal March amount of 21 to 23, companies found that their production and sales for the month were down year-on-year.
This may have prompted them to give a more downbeat assessment of the business climate, Fels said.

Analysts also noted that capacity utilisation in west Germany's manufacturing sector had risen in the first quarter, pointing to strength in the economy. Ifo said capacity usage was 84.9 percent in March, up from 83.2 percent in December.
"I expect the index will rise this year because exports are rolling and the mark has weakened." Fels predicted German GDP will grow three percent, spurred by rising exports and capital investment.
"I wouldn't pin much hope on consumer spending, though. That should only rise one percent."
A weaker mark benefits German exporters because it makes their products cheaper abroad.
